title: Numbers for adults — budgets, bills and roughly how much
goal: Handle the numbers adult life throws at you: millions of rupiah, halves and quarters, percentages, "the third week", "sixty-odd" and "about three million". By the end you can go through a budget at work and sort out the electricity at home.
bekal: say and read large amounts of money: *empat puluh dua setengah juta*, *Rp42,5 juta*, *seribu lima ratus*
use fractions, percentages and ordinals: *setengah*, *seperempat*, *dua pertiga*, *tujuh puluh persen*, *minggu ketiga*

notes: **Empat puluh dua setengah juta** — 42.5 million. *Setengah* (half) slots in after the number it belongs to: *dua setengah juta* is 2.5 million, *satu setengah jam* is an hour and a half. You will also hear *empat puluh dua koma lima juta* ("forty-two comma five"), especially from accountants, because Indonesian writes the decimal point as a comma.

**Sekitar, kira-kira, kurang lebih** all mean "about, roughly". *Sekitar* is neutral, *kira-kira* is a touch more conversational, *kurang lebih* ("less more") is common in reports and meetings. Mbak Nur's *tepatnya* ("to be exact") is the opposite, and entirely in character.

**Padahal** (Unit 12) marks a fact that clashes with what came before: "seventy per cent is gone — and yet it's only the third week". It carries a note of mild alarm or complaint that *tetapi* does not.

**Minggu ketiga, but tanggal dua puluh delapan.** Ordinals are *ke-* + number (*ketiga*, the third), but dates use plain numbers: *tanggal dua puluh delapan*, never *tanggal kedua puluh delapan*. ⚠️ English speakers get this wrong constantly.

**Konsumsi** — literally "consumption" — is office Indonesian for the food and drink at an event: *seksi konsumsi* is the catering committee, and *Konsumsinya apa?* means "what are we feeding people?". *Penawaran* ("offer") is a price quote, and *kuitansi* is a receipt — note the KBBI spelling, not *kwitansi*.

**Mohon … dikumpulkan paling lambat …** is pure Unit 15: the polite passive of office instructions. *Paling lambat* ("at the latest") and its partner *paling cepat* ("at the earliest") are the phrases you will see on every deadline.

grammars.title: Big numbers and money
body: The building blocks are *ribu* (thousand), *juta* (million), *miliar* (billion) and *triliun* (trillion). "One" in front of any of them becomes *se-*: *seribu, sejuta, semiliar* — the same *se-* as Unit 16.
after: ⚠️ Dots and commas are the other way round from English: Indonesian writes 42.500.000 for forty-two and a half million, and 2,5 for two and a half. Read every number twice until your eye adjusts.
*Rupiah* is usually left out when it is obvious; people just say *dua puluh lima ribu*. On price tags and in speech you will also see *rb* for *ribu* and *jt* for *juta*: *25rb*, *2,5 jt*.
💬 In casual speech *ribu* often sounds like *rebu*, and an approximate sum gets *-an*: *Habis sejutaan* ("it came to a million-ish").

grammars.title: Fractions, percentages and ordinals
body: Fractions are built with *per-* ("per, out of"): the top number, then *per-* glued to the bottom number. "One" on top becomes *se-* again.
after: *Pertama* is the one irregular ordinal; after that it is always *ke-* + number: *kedua, ketiga, keempat, kesepuluh, kedua puluh*. The ordinal follows its noun: *minggu ketiga, anak kedua, lantai keempat*.
⚠️ Before a noun, *ke-* means "all": *ketiga anak itu* is "all three children", but *anak ketiga* is "the third child". Position decides.

*Setengahnya*, *sepertiganya*: add *-nya* for "half of it", "a third of it" (Unit 17). *Setengah jam* (half an hour) and *setengah tujuh* (half past six — literally "half seven", a half on the way to seven) you have known since A1.

notes: **Token listrik.** Most Indonesian homes have a prepaid electricity meter: you buy credit (*token*, or *pulsa listrik*) from the state electricity company through an app, a bank or a corner shop, receive a twenty-digit number, and key it into the meter. When the credit runs low the meter beeps — insistently, as every neighbour knows.

**Enam puluhan** — "sixty-something". Add *-an* to a round number and it becomes approximate: *tiga puluhan* (thirty-odd), *umur empat puluhan* (in her forties), *tahun sembilan puluhan* (the nineties). The same *-an* on the units themselves gives "dozens of", "hundreds of" — see the box below.

**Dua kali lipat** — "twice as much, double" (literally "two times fold"). *Tiga kali lipat* is triple. Without *lipat*, *dua kali* just means "twice" as in "two times": *Saya ke sana dua kali* (I went there twice).
**Waduh** is the Javanese-flavoured "oh dear, uh-oh" — a little more dramatic than *aduh*. Both are everywhere, and both are perfectly polite.

**Iuran** is a regular contribution: to the RT for rubbish collection and night security (*keamanan*, often still called *ronda*), to a club, to an office gift fund. It is small, it is collected monthly, and paying it on time is part of being a good neighbour.

**Biar saya yang pencet** — "let me be the one who presses". *Biar* ("let") + *saya yang* + verb is the natural way to offer to do something yourself: *Biar saya yang bayar* (let me pay). *Pencet* is spoken for *memencet*, to press a button.

grammars.title: Roughly how many: approximation
body: Indonesian has a rich kit for vagueness, and in daily life it is used more than exact figures. Each tool has its own place in the sentence.

head: Tool
Example
English
rows: a few thousand, for hours on end

after: *Puluhan, ratusan, ribuan* go straight in front of the noun with no "of": *ribuan orang* (thousands of people), *jutaan rupiah* (millions of rupiah).
⚠️ Eleven to nineteen have their own vague word, *belasan* ("in the teens"): *belasan orang* (a dozen or so people), *anak belasan tahun* (a teenager).

💬 *Kira-kira* at the front of a question means "do you reckon…?", and it makes any request for an estimate sound friendlier: *Kira-kira cukup nggak, Bu?* (Do you think it'll be enough?), *Kira-kira jam berapa sampai?* (Roughly when will you get here?). Indonesians use it constantly with drivers, builders and anyone quoting a price.

blocks.title: Street money in Jakarta
items: Jakarta market slang has Hokkien-origin names for sums: *gopek* (500), *seceng* (1,000), *goceng* (5,000), *ceban* (10,000), *cepek* (100).
In Yogyakarta you will hear them less, but everyone understands them. You do not need to use them; you do need to recognise *goceng*.
*Kembaliannya* is "the change": *Ada kembalian?* — "Have you got change?"

blocks.text: The vocabulary of monthly life. Most of it lives on screens and receipts, so it is baku, and you will read it more often than you say it.

⚠️ *Telat* is the everyday word for *terlambat* (late), and it covers payments as well as people: *Bayarnya telat seminggu* — "the payment was a week late". If you pay by transfer, the phrase you need is *Sudah saya transfer, ya* — "I've transferred it" — ideally followed by a screenshot. Nobody considers a payment real until they have seen the *bukti transfer* (proof of transfer).
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
